title: How Meta is using Instagram to get an ad boost from its Muse personal AI agent
summary: Meta doesn't serve ads in its Muse personal agent, but the tool is already boosting the company's ad business, a senior executive told CNBC.
body: Meta' s ad-free Muse personal artificial intelligence agent is already helping the social media giant boost its advertising business, and it's happening through Instagram, multiple people told CNBC. Instagram is a major advertising revenue engine for the social media giant, and the company is leveraging existing habits on the platform by prompting users to organize their saved posts in Muse. About 20% of daily Instagram users save at least one post to the app per day, according to a person familiar with the details, who asked not to be named because the information is not public. Many of those saved items, the person said, are either shoppable items or ads. A senior executive told CNBC that Muse, even without ads, "is still very valuable for our ads business because it raises conversions for advertisers." It does this by reducing friction in the shopping process and allowing users to go back to items later, said the executive, who asked not to be named because the details have not been reported publicly. "It gives advertisers a way to get more ROI for the dollars they're already spending, and that's all because Muse is helping people shop," the executive said. Mark Zuckerberg announced in Meta's last earnings call that 25% of Muse's users shop via the agentic tool — it's the most common use case for Muse — and the average purchase price is over $200. Zuckerberg said the company plans to take a small fee from transactions made through the agentic platform. All that information about what people are shopping for with their agent is a valuable asset to target ads more precisely within Instagram. If consumers complete purchases with their Muse, that builds Meta's new revenue stream. Meta's efforts to drive transactions seem to be paying off, and the buzz around Muse has made it a leader in agentic shopping. In the week ending Nov. 22, 51% of all agentic orders were done by Meta's Muse, according to transactions measured by Forter Intelligence, an e-commerce analytics and cybertechnology company . Meta dominates agentic AI shopping market share, according to Forter, which said that SpaceX 's Grok held a 24% market share in that same time period, followed by 22% to OpenAI's ChatGPT. The remaining 3% is divided between Google and startup Instinct. Meta is expected to eventually launch ads in Muse, though multiple people said that it's not under any financial pressure to do so and tends to take its time building an audience before monetizing it. The people said that putting ads in the Muse feed, which is more akin to a newsfeed instead of responses to specific queries, would be a natural way for Meta to test ads on the platform.

title: Gold is doing something strange. Here's one way to play it
summary: Gold is not acting like the traditional safe haven. How one trader is playing the move.
body: Gold has stopped trading like a haven and started trading more like a market index this year. The past week has underscored it. Fears around AI, a hawkish Fed, and a stronger dollar sent many investors rushing to raise cash, and gold was sold along with stocks. GLD (SPDR Gold Shares) and the S&P 500 both slid around 9%. Gold then shared in the market's Monday rebound, with GLD up about 3% as the S&P 500 jumped nearly 5%. Over long timeframes, gold's returns tend to move independently of the S&P 500's . From 2004 to 2025, the correlation between their daily returns has been just 0.05 (+1 means the two move in lockstep and -1 means they move in opposite directions). That relationship fluctuates, and 2026 has seen an unusually strong link. The correlation has been about 0.41 so far in 2026. Its rolling three-month reading peaked near 0.80 in June and now sits at 0.54, still higher than about 95% of rolling three-month readings since 2005. Since the end of August, GLD has fallen on 77% of the S&P 500's down days, compared with roughly half historically. The options market is also behaving unusually. Gold options typically price calls richer than puts (call skew). Like other commodities, gold is prone to sharp rallies, and investors use calls to bet on them or hedge against macroeconomic risks. However, gold options have mostly shown the reverse this year, with puts currently trading richer than calls (put skew). It's a sign investors are paying a premium for protection against further declines, which is unusual for gold and more typical of stock options. Those richer puts come as uncertainty around gold runs high heading into December. The PCE inflation report arrives Wednesday, followed by the jobs report next week and the Fed's decision and CPI the week after. GLD's implied volatility, a measure of how much the options market expects the fund to move, is now higher than on about 80% of days over the past year. Options are pricing in an expected move of about 6%, or roughly $20, by Dec. 18. With gold options pricier than usual and puts unusually rich, that presents an interesting setup for traders willing to sell premium. Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the Dec. 18 310/300 put spread and 360/370 call spread in GLD for a credit of roughly $2.24. This is a directionally neutral trade. Gold has been swinging with the market and is down about 33% from its January high. With the Fed and inflation data ahead, it's hard to say whether gold has bottomed or has further to fall into mid-December. A neutral position can collect the elevated premium without picking a direction, and the richer put side adds more. The short strikes sit just outside the range the options market is pricing for Dec. 18, roughly 7% to 8% from Monday's close. That leaves room for a continued selloff or an extended rebound. The trade reaches its maximum profit of $224 if GLD closes between $310 and $360 on Dec. 18. It carries a 62% theoretical probability of profit and can show a gain before expiration if GLD remains relatively rangebound. The maximum loss is capped by the long options and reaches $776 if GLD closes below $300 or above $370, 10% to 11% from Monday's close. Defining risk is especially important with the upcoming catalysts and recent price volatility in gold. GLD has had 30 daily moves of more than 3% this year, including a 10.3% drop on Jan. 30. The trade breaks even at $307.76 on the downside and $362.24 on the upside. A close between $360 and $370 can assign the short call and leave a short position in the fund, so investors looking to avoid that should consider managing the trade before expiration. If GLD finishes between $300 and $310, the short put can be assigned, creating an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $310. After the credit, that's a cost basis of about $307.76, roughly 8% below Monday's close. body: A clear beat on services inflation adds weight to December BOJ hike pricing. That should offer the yen some support and nudge short-dated JGB yields higher, especially if upcoming wage data confirms the pass-through. The yen's response may be limited while the Fed is also on a hiking path , which keeps the rate gap with the US wide and USD/JPY elevated. For equities, firmer BOJ expectations are a headwind for rate-sensitive sectors and exporters, while banks stand to benefit from higher margins. The rise in ocean freight costs is a reminder that Middle East shipping disruption is still feeding through to Asian prices. Japanese companies are paying more for each other's services, with freight, leasing and hotel costs pushing the index to a 4.2% annual rise and giving the BOJ another reason to tighten in December. Prices that Japanese companies charge each other for services rose at a faster pace than expected in October, adding to evidence that inflation is broadening across the economy and strengthening the case for another Bank of Japan rate increase. The services producer price index climbed 4.2% from a year earlier, well above the 3.6% forecast and up from a revised 3.8% in September, according to Bank of Japan data reported by Reuters. The rise was driven largely by higher ocean freight costs, leasing fees and hotel charges. The BOJ watches the index closely as a guide to how far firms are passing rising labour costs on to the prices of services, a key link in its assessment of whether inflation is becoming self-sustaining rather than driven mainly by imported costs. That distinction matters because external pressures remain intense. Stubbornly high energy costs and the rising price of imports, amplified by a weak yen, have kept inflation elevated, and the BOJ has responded by quickening its pace of tightening. It raised its policy rate to 1.25% in September, following a hike in June, a much shorter gap between moves than the roughly twice-yearly increases of 2024 and 2025. Governor Kazuo Ueda has signalled that the bank is ready to keep raising rates to prevent inflation from overshooting its 2% target. A firm services reading supports that stance, suggesting price pressure is no longer confined to goods and energy. Markets and economists are positioned for more. A majority of analysts in a recent poll expect the BOJ to raise rates again in December and follow up with a further increase by the end of March, with many seeing the peak in borrowing costs at around 1.75% to 2.0%. The December policy meeting is now the focus, with upcoming wage and consumer price data likely to shape the timing. body: The headline rise is largely priced in, so the Australian dollar and short-dated Australian government bond yields are more exposed to the core reading. The Aussie is trading around 66.4 US cents. A trimmed mean of 0.4% or firmer would likely lift front-end yields and support the currency by pushing back expectations for the first rate cut. A 0.3% print would leave in place the banks' expected easing timeline for mid-to-late 2027. US markets are heading into a Thanksgiving-shortened week, so any AUD move may meet thinner liquidity than usual. For energy watchers, the fuel-led headline is another sign of crude prices feeding into inflation and central bank decisions well beyond the US. Australia's October consumer price index, due at 00:30 GMT on Wednesday (7:30pm US Eastern on Tuesday), is expected to show headline inflation at what forecasters see as the top of the current cycle. The core reading will shape expectations for when the Reserve Bank of Australia can begin cutting rates. Consensus has headline CPI rising 0.4% over the month, taking the annual rate to 4.8% from 4.3% in September. Forecasts for the trimmed mean, the RBA's preferred core gauge, are less settled. Most calls are at 0.3% m/m with the annual rate holding at 3.6%, while several forecasters see 0.4% and a lift to 3.7%. The big four banks are split down the middle. Commonwealth Bank and NAB both see headline at 4.7% and the trimmed mean steady at 3.6%. Westpac and ANZ are at 4.8% and 3.7%. In its preview, Westpac forecast monthly gains of around 0.4% for both headline and core and described October as the likely peak in Australian inflation, with the trimmed mean expected to slip below 3% by the third quarter of 2027. Fuel does most of the work on the headline. NAB estimates higher automotive fuel prices will add around 1.2 points to year-end inflation, and the unwinding of government electricity subsidies adds to the rise. Neither is the kind of domestic demand pressure that monetary policy is designed to lean against. A wildcard sits in the core: card payment surcharges were banned from 1 October, and it is unclear how many businesses folded that cost into their prices. ANZ estimates the change could add about 0.1 point to headline CPI. The labour market has turned sharply. Unemployment rose to 4.9% in October, its highest since 2021, after a similar upside surprise in September, and the economy shed jobs in both months. At its November meeting the RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, but three of the nine board members preferred to hold, and the statement afterwards no longer flagged further increases. Markets price a hold at the 7 to 8 December meeting as near certain, and all four major banks expect one. That makes today's numbers a guide to the timing of the first cut, which the banks currently place between June and August 2027. A 0.3% core print would support the view that inflation has peaked and keep mid-2027 easing in sight. A 0.4% or firmer reading would suggest underlying price pressure is fading too slowly for the board to ease soon, even as job losses mount. Your market education doesn't end here. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… Oil prices have tumbled by more than 20% so far in November with Brent Crude sinking below $90 per barrel this week, as market participants and analysts bet on continued recovery of crude oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz. The oil market balance appears to be tipping into oversupply, forecasters say, and crude prices are reflecting this notion. But the product markets, especially the diesel market, remain tight, despite recent declines in diesel margins and retail prices. Retail diesel prices in the United States last week fell below $6 per gallon for the first time in over two months, and gasoline prices have also dropped below $4 a gallon in recent weeks amid the slide in crude oil prices. Diesel refining margins, however, remain double or triple compared to before the Iran war, depending on the region, even if they had dropped off from the all-time highs hit in September. The expected glut in the crude oil market is not directly translating into an abundance of diesel supplies. Shipments of diesel from the Middle East remain a fraction compared to before the war, while Russia’s diesel exports have collapsed as Ukraine is regularly taking Russian refineries offline in a massive campaign to cut fuel supply to the front line and export revenues for the Kremlin. Despite their best efforts so far this year, refineries elsewhere cannot fully offset the estimated loss of about 2 million barrels per day (bpd) of total diesel exports from the Middle East and Russia combined. Related: Saudi Arabia Sees Smaller Economic Slump as More Oil Reaches Market Diesel margins, futures, and retail prices have eased this month, and inventories in the U.S. have started to gradually increase, but the market will take months to rebalance, assuming there is no escalation in the Middle East. “The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its Oil Market Report for November. Observed oil inventories rose by 52 million barrels, or by 1.7 million bpd, in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand. The rebound in exports from the Persian Gulf was mostly led by crude oil volumes, the IEA noted. The November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus this quarter, with a more substantial build in 2027, according to the agency. However, diesel tightness persists, and product supply in the diesel market “remains the overriding concern of the broader market and consumers,” the IEA said. James Noel-Beswick, Head of Commodities at Sparta Commodities, last week said that the November builds in diesel stocks would not be enough to materially ease the tight market in the first quarter of 2027. Sparta Commodities still sees “a strong bull case” for early next year, as its analysts “still don’t believe that diesel builds are enough for Q1; a colder winter predicted only adds to this,” Noel-Beswick added. In the United States, diesel margins remain materially higher than gasoline margins. In Europe, the diesel margins have fallen by a third to about $60 per barrel. Yet, this is triple the average diesel margins in 2025. body: The US Senate has launched an investigation into alleged ties between Vice President JD Vance and Vitol regarding an oil-trading contract for Venezuela. The investigation follows a Reuters report from earlier this month, which said the U.S. Vice President had met with a Vitol trader before the U.S. invaded Venezuela. The report, dated November 11, quoted an unnamed source as saying JD Vance had met with a gasoline trader from Vitol named John Addison, whom Reuters described as “an old friend and early financier of his political career” at a ski resort in Montana. The report also cited flight records that put Addison’s private jet and the vice presidential plane at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport at the time. Per the same report, Vance and Addison talked about Venezuela and more specifically, how fast Venezuelan crude could be traded in the event that the United States took control of the country’s oil industry, according to the Reuters source. Both the office of the U.S. Vice President and Addison have denied the report, with the Vitol trader telling Reuters that “And anyone who says so is absolutely making it up because I've never ‌told a single soul that was the case.” Also, according to the report, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright called Addison two days after the United States invaded Venezuela and ousted President Nicolas Maduro to take him to the U.S., taking over Venezuelan oil. Soon after, Vitol and Trafigura received special licenses to trade Venezuelan crude from the Trump administration. Related: Saudi Arabia Sees Smaller Economic Slump as More Oil Reaches Market The Energy Department said Vice President Vance and Secretary Wright never discussed Venezuelan oil sales between themselves, and that Vitol was chosen because it is the world’s largest energy commodity trader. Vitol and Trafigura said they had no advance knowledge of the military operation. Venezuela has exported more than 200 million barrels this year. Both Vitol and Trafigura have declined to disclose the terms of their agreements with state oil company PDVSA, but reports from earlier this year said that the two commodity trading majors had struck a deal with the White House to sell 50 million barrels of Venezuelan crude, valued at some $2 billion at the time, soon after the invasion. Later, the total to be sold by the two commodity majors was hiked twofold, to 100 million barrels. The country’s production of crude has rebounded to 1.2 million barrels daily as of October and could further rise to 1.5 million barrels daily by 2028, according to Rystad Energy . Now, following the November 11 Reuters report, the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee has questioned the official statements made by the Trump administration about the Venezuela oil trade matter and will ask Vice President Vance’s office for a number of documents to be submitted by December 14, Reuters again reported this week. “I write today with serious concern that you may have used your position as Vice President to help a major political donor secure lucrative business opportunities involving Venezuelan oil,” Senator Maggie Hassan, who will chair the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee come January, wrote in a letter to Vance. “Despite denials from your office and Mr. Addison, flight records place his private ‌jet and your government plane at the same Montana airport on the day of the reported meeting,” Hassan also wrote. Vance’s office has issued a formal denial that a meeting ever took place, referring to it, however, as “The alleged airport meeting”. Reuters noted in its report it never said the meeting took place at the airport. Meanwhile, John Addison let Vitol in March and is currently the co-chair of the Secretary of Energy Advisory Board along with GE Vernova chief executive Scott Strazik. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States rose 126,000 barrels in the week ending November 20—the last count before the Thanksgiving holiday. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories rose by 5.3 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 49 million barrels over the last 32 weeks, but have gained 1.7 million over the course of this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending November 20, another 2.9 million barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 273.5 million barrels —a level that is 440 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. Abbott effectively froze new data center grid connections in August, then told the agency in September to stop issuing air and other permits for the same projects, and within days it had mailed preliminary approvals for three gas-fired power projects meant to supply data centers, according to a FracTracker and Public Citizen report . title: Tudor sees $2.3B value in Treaty Creek mine
summary: The Goldstorm mine, about 930 km northwest of Vancouver, could produce 4.68 million oz. of gold over 28 years with a 20% internal rate of return.
body: The Goldstorm mine, about 930 km northwest of Vancouver, could produce 4.68 million oz. of gold over 28 years with a 20% internal rate of return. The Treaty Creek gold camp in northwest British Columbia. Credit: Tudor Gold Corp. Tudor Gold’s (TSXV: TUD; US-OTC: TDRRF) Goldstorm deposit in northwestern British Columbia could yield a $2.3 billion (C$3.2 billion) post-tax net present value at $1.54 billion in initial costs, the first economic assessment of its Treaty Creek project shows. The Goldstorm mine, about 930 km northwest of Vancouver, could produce 4.68 million oz. of gold over 28 years with a 20% internal rate of return. “We expect to receive our underground exploration permit in time to collar the portal and begin to excavate the decline in 2027,” Tudor President and CEO Joe Ovsenek said in a release. “With underground access to the Goldstorm deposit we can more efficiently infill drill and expand the higher-grade mineralization.” The drilling would help pin down how much of the richer rock Tudor can count on, a significant task after the PEA. The junior miner must still secure permits and find financing for a project whose initial cost is more than nine times its market capitalization. Goldstorm’s 13.6 million inferred tonnes account for 14% of the 97.8 million tonnes in the mine plan but 29% of its gold. They grade 3.78 grams gold per tonne, more than twice the mine average of 1.8 grams gold. Tudor has yet to declare reserves. Goldstorm’s November 2025 estimate outlined 912.3 million indicated tonnes grading 0.85 gram gold, 5.07 grams silver and 0.15% copper. That amounts to 24.9 million oz. of gold, 148.7 million oz. silver and 3.05 billion lb. copper. Tudor shares fell 4.9% to C58¢ in Toronto on Tuesday afternoon, valuing the company at C$240 million ($168 million). Tudor owns 80% of Treaty Creek and covers exploration costs for its 20% partner, Teuton Resources (TSXV: TUO; US-OTC: TEUTF), until it gives notice of production. Tudor would feed its 10,000-tonne-a-day mill from four zones, starting with some of the richest material. Gold output would average 202,300 oz. annually from years three through 12, at the low end of the 200,000 to 300,000 oz. range management was targeting in October. The life-of-mine average would be 165,600 oz. a year. Vancouver-based Fuse Advisors assumed $3,670 per oz. gold, $50 per oz. silver and $5 per lb. copper. At those prices, the mine would pay back its initial costs in 3.7 years. Over its life, the mine would also yield 22.1 million oz. of silver and 209,900 tonnes of copper. After credits for both metals, all-in sustaining costs would average $1,358 per oz. of gold. Tudor is looking to Perfectstorm, about 1 km west of Goldstorm, to lift early gold output. Hole PS-26-36 cut 9 grams gold over 9.5 metres from 163.5 metres downhole, Tudor reported Nov. 11. If next year’s drilling supports an initial resource by year-end, Tudor plans to study how to bring Perfectstorm into production. The proposed mill and some underground workings overlap with a provincial licence of occupation held by Seabridge Gold (TSX: SEA; NYSE: SA) for its neighbouring KSM project. Tudor may have to move or redesign those facilities unless the companies reach an agreement or the province changes the tenure, the study says. B.C. has deferred a decision on permits for the full length of Seabridge’s proposed ore tunnels. About 12.5 km of the route crosses Tudor’s claims, passing through Goldstorm and Perfectstorm, Tudor says. In a separate ruling , the B.C. Supreme Court confirmed last week that it had quashed the province’s finding that KSM construction had “substantially started.” B.C. must consult the Tsetsaut Skii km Lax Ha Nation in depth before making a new decision. KSM’s environmental certificate remains in force during the review, Seabridge said.

title: Bitcoin (BTC) Price Prediction: Bearish structure holds as ETF outflows and weak trend pressure Bitcoin lower - Blockchain News
body: Bitcoin’s tape is weak, and the market backdrop around it is worse. On Binance spot, BTC was last quoted at $60,424.69, down 1.74% on the day and sitting well below its 7-day, 20-day, 50-day and 200-day moving averages. The technical stack is plainly bearish: SMA 7 at $61,026.99 is below SMA 20 at $67,606.24, which is below SMA 50 at $75,750.00, while RSI at 25.36 is in oversold territory and the MACD reading remains negative. That combination usually signals downside momentum first, with any bounce more likely to be a reaction than a trend reversal unless price can reclaim higher resistance quickly. The flow backdrop reinforces that message. The Block reported on November 23, 2026 that U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.79 billion of net outflows in the prior week, the largest weekly withdrawal since late June, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for $1.37 billion of that total. The same report said outflows were becoming “structural” and noted that total bitcoin ETF assets had fallen to $71.35 billion from about $110 billion. That matters because ETF demand has been one of the cleaner liquidity channels into BTC; persistent redemptions can keep pressure on spot even when intraday indicators look washed out. The nearest chart reference points are close enough to matter. Bitcoin’s immediate support is $58,385.63, with strong support at $56,346.56. Immediate resistance sits at $63,533.44, and stronger resistance at $66,642.18. The 24-hour trading range of $64,603.12 to $59,455.31 shows that sellers are still defending rallies rather than allowing a clean mean reversion. Volatility is elevated but not chaotic. BTC’s 14-day ATR is $3,390.80, which means intraday and multi-session swings can remain wide even if open interest is not expanding aggressively. Binance futures data show open interest value at $5.70 billion, down 0.25% over 24 hours, with funding rate essentially neutral at 0.0028%. That combination suggests the move is not being powered by a heavily crowded new levered long build-up or a sharp short squeeze; instead, it looks more like a position-clearing decline under weak spot demand. The Binance global long/short ratio was 2.6792 at 06:00 UTC, and top traders were even more tilted long at 2.9698 at 07:00 UTC. The taker buy/sell ratio was 1.0238, close to balanced. Those readings show that Binance cohorts are still leaning long, but they do not prove conviction, and they do not override the spot trend. In practice, a long-skewed derivatives book against a falling spot market can become fuel for further liquidations if support breaks, especially when the broader flow picture is already negative. The bullish case from current levels is not about chasing momentum; it is about a failed breakdown and a reclaim of lost structure. BTC would need to stabilize above the immediate support band and then retake $63,533.44 to reduce downside pressure. A stronger repair would require a move back through $66,642.18 and, more importantly, evidence that ETF outflows are slowing rather than persisting. The bearish case remains straightforward. If Bitcoin loses $58,385.63 decisively, the next layer of support is $56,346.56, and the market would be leaning more heavily on oversold conditions rather than on improving flows. The evidence from Wintermute, cited by CoinDesk on November 17, 2026, also fits that risk-off framing: the firm warned BTC could slide into the $50,000s after losing its 200-week average near $68,000, pointing to negative flows and weaker demand as headwinds. Citi’s November 18 target cut to $99,532 is still far above spot, but that is a 12-month valuation view, not a short-term trading floor, and it does not cancel the current tape damage.

BHP’s Copper Growth Plan Looks Pricey To Analysts - Finimize
body: Berenberg kept a hold rating, warning that $13.6-17.4 billion of capex and block cave execution risks could weigh on free cash flow and dividends. After touring BHP’s Copper South Australia operations, Berenberg, a European investment bank, stuck with its hold rating: the miner’s copper growth plan looks strategically sound, but expensive enough to squeeze near-term cash returns. BHP wants to lift copper output about 40% to 2 million tonnes a year by fiscal 2035, from roughly 1.4 million tonnes in 2026, with much of the growth tied to its Copper South Australia projects. Berenberg’s concern is the funding bridge: it estimates $13.6-17.4 billion of capital spending across the two phases and points to “block cave” mining, a technique that undercuts ore from below, as a source of schedule an.. Those extra dollars matter because BHP itself expects copper “capital intensity” (how much spending it takes to add a tonne of capacity) to rise to about $27,000 per tonne over 2026-35 from about $20,000 over 2021-25. In plain terms, even if copper prices cooperate, more of the business’s cash could be tied up in construction, contingencies, and rework before it ever shows up as free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital spending). That’s why Berenberg can call the plan “compelling” while still trimming some forecasts and keeping a 35-pound price target on the London-listed shares. For markets: Berenberg’s $13.6-17.4 billion capex range puts dividends on a construction schedule. For income-focused shareholders, the debate is less about the end goal of 2 million tonnes by fiscal 2035 and more about what happens during the build. Higher capital intensity means each incremental dollar of copper revenue has a bigger job to do: fund expansion first, then support buybacks and dividends. Add in block cave execution risk, and investors may start treating BHP’s near-term dividend outlook as a project-delivery question: delays or overruns can pull cash forward into spending, while smooth execution leaves more room for payouts. title: Glencore Keeps Deutsche Bank's Buy Rating Despite Trimmed Target as Copper Bet Outweighs Near-Term H - ad-hoc-news.de
body: Deutsche Bank has reaffirmed its buy recommendation on Glencore while trimming its price target to 620 pence from 680 pence, drawing a deliberate line between short-term earnings pressure and the miner's longer-term production story. The move reflects softer commodity prices and broader economic headwinds weighing on profit expectations — but the positive rating rests on copper growth and the prospect of richer shareholder returns. The distinction matters for investors. The lower target accounts for gloomier earnings prospects, while the buy call leans on opportunities beyond those near-term drags. A clean bill of health for current trading cannot be inferred from the positive verdict. For 2026 and 2027, the German bank is cutting its profit forecasts by an average of 6%. Those reduced estimates capture the strain from a weaker commodities environment; they are not company-reported results from Glencore itself. On the other side of the ledger, Deutsche Bank expects copper prices to recover in 2027, citing sustained global economic growth as support. That expectation complements the company-specific thesis: it isn't only higher output, but a more favourable pricing backdrop that could brighten Glencore's outlook. According to the analysts, Glencore aims to lift annual copper production to 1 million tonnes by 2028. At the announced investor update on 7 December, revised multi-year guidance is expected to take centre stage, alongside details on investment, costs and possible asset sales. Judging the growth goal therefore requires more than the targeted tonnage — the spending earmarked for it and the trajectory of costs matter just as much. Only together do these figures allow an assessment of how attractive the production build-out could prove for shareholders. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Glencore? Deutsche Bank views the copper growth potential over the next 12–18 months as underestimated. In its assessment, potential asset disposals could also pave the way for higher shareholder returns in 2027. Both remain expectations, not commitments. The next concrete test of the buy case is thus the promised production and investment guidance, which must show how Glencore intends to fund the copper expansion while still leaving room for shareholders. The reassessment lands after a strong session for the stock. Glencore climbed 6.5% yesterday amid a recovery in mining shares, with gold and copper prices rebounding after the previous week's declines, according to Reuters. Mining stocks helped prop up the British equity market. On 19 November, Glencore committed to take up to 25,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium hydroxide annually under an expanded offtake agreement with Tees Valley Lithium — a volume matching the entire planned capacity of the first production line. The arrangement was struck between a Glencore subsidiary and Tees Valley Lithium, a unit of Alkemy Capital Investments, and covers offtake from a planned production line. Glencore at a turning point? Under its repurchase programme, Glencore bought back 6.6 million of its own shares from UBS AG at a gross CHF 5.4424 per share. The stock is earmarked for cancellation, and the programme is expected to conclude by February 2027. body: Crude oil futures turned lower in Asian trading on the morning of the 25th, giving back part of the previous day's gains. Expectations of rising supply and a shift toward oversupply are outweighing caution over Middle East tensions. As of 10:37 a.m. Japan time (8:37 p.m. EST on Nov. 24), Brent crude futures were down 43 cents, or 0.5%, at $90.97 a barrel (approximately ¥14,000). U.S. WTI futures were down 47 cents, or 0.6%, at $81.58 (approximately ¥13,000). Both benchmarks had just posted gains of more than 2% on the 24th. Weighing on prices is the supply-demand outlook the International Energy Agency (IEA) released on the 13th. The IEA expects the global oil market to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter, citing the recovery of exports from the Middle East at a pace exceeding global demand growth. Still, Middle East risk is cushioning the downside. Attacks on ships continue in the Strait of Hormuz, and exchanges of fire between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis are ongoing. Takeshi Ueno, senior economist at NLI Research Institute, noted that since the IEA report was published, the perception of a global supply surplus has kept prices in check, while adding that ship attacks around the Strait of Hormuz and fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis "are heightening uncertainty over the sustainability of this trend." Supply-side factors are notably volatile. The chairman of Libya's National Oil Corp (NOC) said the pipeline at the Sharara oil field, which armed groups had shut by closing valves, has restarted, and oil has begun flowing to storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya. China and India are expected to increase imports of Russian crude to record levels this year, filling the supply gap created by the Iran war. Attention is on the OPEC+ ministerial meeting scheduled for the 29th. The group is expected to decide production policy for 2027, and according to four people familiar with the matter, Iraq is asking OPEC+ to raise the estimate of its crude production capacity. Tensions are rising over the capacity assessment that will shape next year's country quotas. Inventory data that reflects actual supply-demand conditions are also bearish. According to market participants citing American Petroleum Institute (API) data, U.S. crude inventories rose by 126,000 barrels in the week through the 20th. A Reuters survey of eight analysts had forecast an average increase of about 1.5 million barrels, and if official data confirm a build, it is likely to cap further gains in prices. Note: Prices are as of 10:37 a.m. Japan time on the 25th. Yen equivalents are for reference only. If crude prices continue to swing between oversupply expectations and geopolitical risk, moves in energy-related stocks and commodity-linked currencies are also likely to remain unstable. The outcome of OPEC+ talks on production policy and Iraq's capacity assessment will be the focal point determining next year's supply-demand balance. title: Treasury yields are steady as investors await more economic data - CNBC
body: U.S. Treasury yields were steady on Tuesday as investors looked ahead to more economic data releases due out later in the week. The 10-year Treasury yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, student loans and credit card debt — was up more than 1 basis point at 4.932%. The 2-year Treasury note yield , the most sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was higher by more than 2 basis points at 4.691%. The 30-year Treasury yield — which often reacts the most to geopolitical developments — rose 2 basis points to 5.315%. One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. The October reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index, which measures underlying inflation, is due Wednesday. A rise of 0.3% is expected, according to economists polled by Dow Jones, with the annual headline inflation anticipated to come in at 3.8%. The data comes after consumer confidence jumped in November. The Conference Board's survey released Tuesday showed the headline confidence index moved to 103.3, marking an increase of 11.4 points from October and above the Dow Jones forecast for 92.2. Also on Tuesday, investors digested the results of a 5-year Treasury auction, which showed slightly soft demand. On Monday, John Williams of the New York Fed said that monetary policy will need to adjust to "get inflation back to our 2% goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis." "There is still work to do to get that done," Williams added in comments at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. He said the latest economic data shows "the economy has remained strong and that inflation has continued to run too high." Williams's comments come ahead of the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee. Investors are now pricing in a 100% chance of another interest rate hike, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool, with a 25 basis point increase expected.
